newsitem.title: DENMARK: Russia seeking entry into East Asian gas market.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeking entry into East Asian gas market.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, June 11, Reuter - Russia has ambitious plans to enter the East Asian natural gas market, and intends to have infrastructure in place to supply the market by 2005 when LNG supplies are no longer sufficient, Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev told a conference here on Wednesday.

Vyakhirev said that estimates showed demand in the region was likely to rise to between 180 billion cubic metres (bcm) and 200 bcm by 2005. In the short term, he said this demand could be met by imports of LNG, but "after 2005-2007 they appear to need new sources of gas. Russia may become one of such sources".

He added that plans included building a new gas production centre in Irkutsk in Siberia "beyond the year 2000." This will initially supply the city of Irkutsk, but he said later, by using this production base and nearby gas fields in Yakutia, it would be possible to link the region with China, North and South Korea, and "very likely" Japan.
He added that on Sakhalin island, north of Japan, Gazprom planned to produce 20 bcm by 2010, of which half would be exported.

After 2010, he said, gas streams from around Irkutsk and from Sakhalin would become the basis of a unified gas transportation system of East Russia, exporting up to 50 bcm annually to Asia-Pacific countries.
Gazprom is also expanding its exports west, he said. He expected that countries in eastern Europe would overcome recession and demand would increase by up to 40 bcm by 2010 as compared with 1995.
"We are aware that gas from the Middle East may start competing with Russian gas in the region in the next 10 to 15 years. But Gazprom expects the Russian gas to win the competition."

Russia is building a pipeline from the Yamal peninsula in northern Russia through Belarus and Poland to Germany, has signed an agreement to build a pipeline to Turkey, and is considering a link through Finland, Sweden and Denmark to reach western and central Europe.

Currently, Vyakhirev said, 66 percent of gas produced in Russia is consumed locally, 20 percent exported to central, south-east and western Europe, and 14 percent exported to the CIS and Baltic countries. Domestic demand is expected to rise from 340 bcm in 1995 to 486 bcm by 2015, he added.
